stances.claim: The cases initiated by the Aquino administration under its daang matuwid anticorruption program will not be finally decided when he ends his term on June 30, 2016 -- this is the inevitable conclusion reached by CJ's last three columns

There is one exception -- the ouster of CJ Renato Corona was completed on May 29, 2012 when the Senate issued its guilty verdict; the judgment was instantly final and Corona relinquished office without challenging via SC certiorari
However, Corona's tax-evasion and perjury raps, like all the other daang matuwid filings including the second and third batches of PDAF cases, will not be finally resolved by June 30, 2016

Daang matuwid's future will rest on the new president to be elected on May 9, 2016 -- though the Ombudsman and SC are deeply involved, investigation, prosecution, and speedy resolution will depend largely on the new president

First, the new president will appoint a new DOJ Secretary and a new Solicitor General -- the daang matuwid cases were initiated, investigated, and filed by the DOJ Secretary; evidence preservation and WPP immunity were under her; a new lackadaisical DOJ Secretary or SolGen will mean death for these cases

Second, Ombudsman Carpio-Morales will end her seven-year term on July 28, 2018 with the Constitution barring reappointment -- by her retirement the cases she nurtured will probably not yet mature to final judgment; her successor will need 'big feet to fit into the big shoes she would leave'

Recall that the Estrada plunder case took six years of continuous SBN trial before judgment; had he appealed to the SC instead of accepting a pardon, the case would have dragged on a few more years -- illustrating the time-frame for plunder-class cases

Third, 11 of the 15 incumbent SC justices will reach compulsory retirement age of 70 during the next president's six-year term -- justices are expected to be independent of the appointing authority, but a president always appoints magistrates to propel his/her vision of governance

A new president passionate in pursuing the anticorruption campaign will naturally name magistrates as passionate in ridding society of graft -- justices have wide discretion in determining probable cause, strong evidence, or proof beyond reasonable doubt; even in the US, the appointment of new justices is dependent on ideological compatibility (Republicans appoint conservatives, Democrats choose liberals -- see CJ's July 12 and 19, 2015 columns)

11 retiring justices: Villarama (April 14, 2016), Perez (Dec 14, 2016), Brion (Dec 29, 2016); Reyes (July 6, 2017), Mendoza (Aug 13, 2017); Velasco (Aug 8, 2018), De Castro (Oct 8, 2018); del Castillo (July 29, 2019), Jardeleza (Sept 26, 2019), Bersamin (Oct 18, 2019), Carpio (Oct 26, 2019)

Only Sereno, Peralta, Bernabe, and Leonen will not be replaced by the next president -- Peralta (March 27, 2022) and Bernabe (May 14, 2022) retirements fall within the prohibited midnight-appointment window (two months before next presidential elections up to end of term); the same bar precludes P-Noy from naming Villarama's successor unless Villarama retires voluntarily early

With prudent use of his/her appointing power, the new president could change the face of the SC, which in turn could effect sweeping reforms in our justice system -- neutralizing the four 'ACID' problems that corrode justice: Access to justice by the poor, Corruption, Incompetence of some judges, Delay in delivery of quality justice
Like the economy, judicial reforms need time and effort to mature, bear fruit, and become truly inclusive

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a strategic outlook on the 'daang matuwid' anticorruption program's future. The cases initiated by Aquino's daang matuwid (straight path) program will not be finally decided when he ends his term on June 30, 2016 -- the inevitable conclusion reached by CJ's last three columns. There is one exception: the ouster of then-CJ Renato Corona was completed on May 29, 2012 when the Senate issued its guilty verdict, instantly final; Corona relinquished office without challenging via SC certiorari. However, his tax-evasion and perjury raps, like all other daang matuwid filings including the PDAF second and third batches, will not be finally resolved by June 30, 2016. What will happen to all these cases? On a broader scale, what is the future of the straight path? Where will it lead? 'Quo vadis daang matuwid?' Daang matuwid's future will rest on the new president to be elected on May 9, 2016 -- though the Ombudsman and SC are deeply involved, investigation, prosecution, and speedy resolution will depend largely on the new president. 'Let me count the reasons.' First, the new president will appoint a new Secretary of Justice and a new Solicitor General. The daang matuwid cases were initiated, investigated, and filed by the DOJ Secretary in the Ombudsman or in the courts; the DOJ Secretary gathered and preserved evidence and granted immunity to key witnesses under the Witness Protection Program. If the new DOJ Secretary will not tend to the cases diligently, they will probably 'wither and die.' The SolGen is counsel of DOJ and Ombudsman when cases reach the appellate courts; a lackadaisical SolGen will also mean death for these cases. Second, Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales will end her seven-year term on July 28, 2018; the Constitution bars reappointment. Being solely responsible for filing and prosecuting graft cases against top officials, the new appointee's courage, independence, diligence, and probity will be crucial. By Morales' retirement, the cases she nurtured will probably not yet mature to final judgment -- her successor will need 'big feet to fit into the big shoes she would leave.' Recall that the SBN Special Division took six years of continuous trial before judging Estrada's plunder; had he appealed to the SC instead of accepting a pardon, the case would have dragged a few more years. Third, 11 of the 15 incumbent SC justices will reach compulsory retirement age of 70 during the next president's six-year term -- the next president will therefore name their replacements. Justices are expected to be independent of the appointing authority, but a president always appoints magistrates to propel his/her vision of governance. A new president passionate in pursuing the anticorruption campaign will naturally name magistrates as passionate in ridding society of graft. Justices have wide discretion in determining probable cause, strong evidence, or proof beyond reasonable doubt -- this is why they often disagree. Even in the US, appointment of new justices is dependent on ideological compatibility: Republicans appoint 'conservatives,' Democrats choose 'liberals' (see CJ's July 12 and 19, 2015 columns). The 11 retiring justices: in 2016 -- Martin Villarama Jr. (April 14), Jose Perez (Dec 14), Arturo Brion (Dec 29); in 2017 -- Bienvenido Reyes (July 6), Jose Mendoza (Aug 13); in 2018 -- Presbitero Velasco Jr. (Aug 8), Teresita De Castro (Oct 8); in 2019 -- Mariano del Castillo (July 29), Francis Jardeleza (Sept 26), Lucas Bersamin (Oct 18), Antonio Carpio (Oct 26). Only CJ Sereno, Justices Peralta, Bernabe, and Leonen will not be replaced by the new president. Peralta will retire on March 27, 2022 and Bernabe on May 14, 2022, within the last few months of the new president's term -- but the Constitution bars any appointment 'two months immediately before the next presidential elections up to the end of (the president's) term.' The same bar on 'midnight appointments' precludes P-Noy from naming Villarama's successor (April 14, 2016, within the two-month prohibition) -- though Villarama can retire voluntarily ahead of this period, allowing P-Noy to appoint his successor. Clearly, with prudent use of appointing power, the new president could change the face of the SC, which in turn could effect sweeping reforms in our justice system. It takes both people and system to neutralize the 'ACID' problems that corrode justice: (1) Access to justice by the poor, (2) Corruption, (3) Incompetence of some judges, (4) Delay in the delivery of quality justice. Like the economy, judicial reforms need time and effort to mature, bear fruit, and become truly inclusive.
